units: two different routes lead to the same high crossing point
one of them climbs a steep face whose ground is covered with stones
on that steep route the walkers move upward in tight zigzags
the other route loops round a soft rolling landform
the gentle route is half as long again as the steep one
its steady gradient makes it possible to hold an even pace
workers record the height, the width and the type of ground every season
on the steep way timber steps are set and held by driven pegs
on the gentle way channels are cut to run the water off
a heavily loaded walker will take the less steep way
text: Two separate paths reach the same high saddle, and the two could hardly be less alike. One takes on a steep face where the ground lies loose with stones, so walkers work upward in tight zigzags, planting each boot flat on the tilted slabs. The other swings round a soft rolling shoulder of hillside. It runs half as long again, yet the gradient never changes, and that lets a walker hold a single steady pace from bottom to top. The crews who look after both routes measure the rise, the usable width and the make-up of the ground before every season. On the steep line they set timber steps and hold them with driven pegs. On the gentle line they cut side channels so the water runs off. Anyone carrying a heavy load will pick the easier gradient; anyone racing the mist to the ridge will not.

units: the writer looks into the reasons that push people to go far away
he lists three motives shared by most travellers
the first is the change of setting, which sharpens the attention
the second is the exchange with those who live in the place
the writer holds conversation to be worth more than looking alone
the third motive consists in piling up places visited
this piling up is criticised because it turns a site into a catch
the writer advises going more slowly and staying put
he proposes giving up bringing back any trace of the journey
text: It is worth asking what we are really after when we cross into distant country. Three motives turn up in most travellers. The first is the shift of setting: you leave a familiar backdrop for a horizon whose rules you do not know, and your attention sharpens at once. The second is exchange. An hour of talk with a herder, a fisherman or a weaver is worth more than gazing at one grand view after another. The third is harder to own up to, and it amounts to collecting: places are stacked up the way others stack picture cards. That last motive deserves hard scrutiny, since it turns a clear valley into a trophy and the traveller into a book-keeper of his own feats. A decent way of moving through the world would mean slowing down, staying put, and carrying home no proof at all.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman described leads walkers in the mountains
her father raised livestock
she spent her childhood in an isolated cluster of houses
very young, she drove the animals along waterlogged paths
she went through a training where she learnt to read maps
that training also covered rescue on difficult ground
she came back qualified to her valley to guide visitors there
she can judge a party's exhaustion from the way it walks
she now trains future guides
she says the only thing she misses of her father's work is the smell of fodder
text: The woman who leads walkers into the high country grew up as a stock-breeder's daughter, in a cluster of houses where the road gave out at the last meadow. She was still small when she began driving the animals along tracks that ran with water, and she learnt to read the sky before the other children did. As a girl she left for a training school, where maps became a language to her and where she was taught to bring an injured body off broken ground. She came home with her certificate and offered herself to the walkers passing through. Ten seasons of that taught her to gauge a party's exhaustion from its gait alone. Now she trains guides herself: how slopes read, where to halt, how to announce that a summit must be given up. Of her father's trade she misses only the smell of cut fodder.

units: the speaker was let down by a walk along the sea
the leaflet announced a shore left in its wild state
the path has in fact been widened to let machines through
a barrier runs the whole length of the route
that barrier hides the drop and removes the sense of danger
the walker ends up watching the ground instead of the landscape
the gravel surface turns dangerous under fine rain
the final part of the route becomes narrow and wild again
the speaker finds there the interest he had expected from the outing
text: Honestly, that walk along the coast let me down, and it took me a good while to work out why. The leaflet had promised a shoreline left wild. What you actually get is a track widened for maintenance machinery, with a railing running the whole way along it. Because the railing blocks the drop, the sense of exposure goes, and exposure is the whole point of walking a cliff edge. So you push on quickly, you watch your feet, and there is nothing left to fear or to admire. Add to that the gravel they have laid down: it turns slippery the moment a light drizzle sets in, so you brake the whole way without getting anything back for it. Only the very last stretch rescues the outing. There the path narrows down again, a heavy sea batters the rocks, and you get at last what brought you out.

units: the writer of the message is staying at a mountain inn
the local economy depends on walkers coming
rainfall has brought down a long stretch of the usual path
bookings were cancelled and the lodging emptied
a solution was found after three evenings of argument
the women of the place suggested a replacement route on the other flank
a woodworker is building a log crossing over a boggy hollow
the postal worker drew the new route on a public map
the walkers came back the following week
text: I am writing to you from an inn up the valley, and I will set out what has happened here as a reporter would. The hamlet lives off passing walkers, and after the rains a long stretch of the main path slid away. Visitors called off their bookings, the rooms emptied, and the innkeeper began talking about a lost season. A way out took shape over three evenings of argument. It was the women of the place who put forward a replacement route along the shaded flank, longer but sound underfoot. A carpenter is building a log crossing over the boggy hollow. The postman, who knows every short cut in the district, has marked the altered route on a map pinned up at the entrance to the village. The walkers were back within the week. I leave tomorrow by that path and will tell you how it holds up.

units: the question asked sets the sea edges against the summits
an old walker answers by asking what one wants from walking
he links flat expanses with the loss of oneself
he explains that flat ground strips away the landmarks
he links the summits with physical hardship
effort high up hands the walker back the feel of his skeleton
he is asked which setting leaves the most lasting trace
he chooses the emptiest setting, since it offers little to memorise
he sets that emptiness against a rich valley that scatters into small details
he holds that one never finds the place as one left it
text: Shore or summit, which is the better ground for walking? An old walker used to meet the question with one of his own: what is it you want from walking? If it is the loss of yourself, he said, take the flats, since a level expanse strips away every landmark and lets the mind drift under a low sky. If it is the ordeal you want, the ridge wins. Every step up there is paid for, and the effort hands the walker back the feel of his own bones. He was asked next which of the two settings prints itself deeper on the memory. He chose the barer one without pausing: a naked expanse, no tree, no roof, stays with you because it gives you so little to hold, whereas a fertile valley crumbles into small particulars. The last question was about going back. You never return, he smiled, to the place you left.

units: a rock specialist teaches how to examine a slope before climbing it
a rock that splits into thin leaves lets water work its way in
that kind of ground becomes dangerous after rain
a slope held by shrubs stands up better than a slope without plants
the roots pin down the loose part of the ground
a flank kept from the sun holds its water for longer
flat shelves on a slope show where earth has slipped in the past
a member of the party asks the specialist about gullies that look dry
the answer is that a stony bed fills with water in a downpour
the closing advice is to avoid any steep slope whose exit cannot be seen
text: The rock specialist showed the party how to read a slope before committing to it. He began with the stone itself. Where it splits into thin leaves, he said, water works its way in, and the ground turns treacherous once rain has fallen. He moved on to what grows there: a slope held by shrubs stands up better than a bare bank, because the roots pin down the loose layer. He noted in passing that a flank kept out of the sun holds its wet long after the rest has dried. Last came the shape of the ground, and he dwelt on the flat shelves, which mark where earth has already slipped. Someone asked whether a gully can be trusted when it looks dry. Not at all, he answered: a stony bed fills in one downpour. His closing advice was to go round any steep passage whose exit you cannot see.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: high crossings first served practical needs
carriers of goods opened the first ways over
those ways took up the lines worn by the herds
builders then put up works spanning the watercourses
those works cut several weeks off the journeys
travel remained the business of merchants and of those who carried letters
scholars later climbed the summits out of pure curiosity
their published accounts created a taste for steep country
the earlier generation found that country ugly
the boring of tunnels did away with the hardship of the crossing
text: Crossing a high pass began as a matter of need, never of pleasure. The first ways over were opened by carriers hauling salt and wool, who followed the lines of least effort that the herds had already worn into the ground. Bridge-builders came after them, able to throw an arch over a torrent and cut weeks from a journey. Even so, the route stayed the business of merchants and of the men who carried letters. Then came scholars who set out to climb the summits from curiosity alone, with instruments and notebooks, and who were taken at first for men who had lost their way. Their accounts, once printed and passed round, gave rise to a fresh taste for broken country that their fathers had thought plainly ugly. In the end the mountain was bored through, and the pass stopped being an ordeal.

units: the clearness of a high lake comes from what its water carries
lowland rivers drag along silt torn from farmed banks
those fine grains hang in the water and get in the way of sight
high up, the ground feeding the lake is short and the rock is hard
the water therefore lifts very little material
the cold holds back the spread of microscopic plants
that scarcity of algae raises the clearness of the water further
a walker sees the stones on the bottom and misjudges the depth
the want of food makes living things rare and fish grow very slowly
works upstream can cloud the water for a whole season
text: A mountain lake looks clear for one reason: what its water is carrying. Rivers down in the lowlands drag along silt torn from farmed banks, and those fine grains hang in the water and blur whatever you try to look at. Higher up, the ground that feeds the lake is short and the rock beneath it hard, so the water lifts almost nothing on its way down. The cold up there plays its part as well. Microscopic plants barely multiply, and their scarcity clears the water further still. A walker can pick out every pebble on the bottom and takes a deep basin for a shallow dip. There is a price for that clearness: with so little to feed on, living things are few and the fish put on weight at a crawl. One dig upstream, stirring the mud of an old deposit, will cloud the lake for a whole season.

units: two walkers meant to cross a flat windswept expanse without a halt
they had set out with little gear
a thick veil of vapour came down halfway across
the route was marked by small piles of stones
those markers became impossible to see
one of the two was for pressing on by guesswork
the narrator refused because of holes where one can be hurt
they worked out a way of moving in which one waits while the other explores
the one going ahead calls out as soon as he makes out the next marker
the veil lifted by a grassy hollow, close to the shelter
text: We had it in our heads to cross the windy tableland in one go, light packs, the map folded in a pocket. Bad reckoning: halfway over, the fog dropped all at once and the line of small stone piles that marked the route simply went. My companion was for pressing on by guesswork. I would not have it, because ground like that is pitted with holes, and a foot goes into one and a bone goes with it. So we made up a method of our own. One of us stayed put at the last marker he could see while the other walked straight ahead to the edge of the murk, shouting as he went. The moment he made out the next pile he called, and his mate came up to him. We worked our way across like that, relay by relay, all afternoon. The fog lifted at a grassy hollow, and the hut stood there within earshot.
